beats.narration_text: Namaste. This is Liam, in for Bear. This is Blackridge: No Way Back, a narrative crime game where you drive freight through a rainy industrial town at night, built in Godot. The prompt on screen is a reconstruction; the real work started from a written brief. Let's take apart the two shaders this build added, and how each one was checked.

beats.narration_text: Blackridge already had the van, the district and the driving. This build adds four pieces: a shader whose colour comes from the van's state, a textured shader shared by two materials, an experiment on what texture hints do to the numbers, and a close reading of the shader Godot generates itself. The game runs Godot four point seven point two, on the Compatibility renderer. Remember that.

beats.role_note: Specification shown verbatim from CHANGE-BRIEF.md (outside game/, so not a gamedev excerpt).
beats.narration_text: Before any shader code, a written brief fixed the contract: the exact colour line, three uniforms, and rules a test can fail. Fade on in a quarter of a second, and off in zero point three five. A retrigger reverses from the current value. One frame of tolerance at 30, 60 and 144 frames per second. The commit history shows the brief landed before the first shader, and the project's Claude dot M D imports it.

beats.role_note: Code beat: the hand-written effect shader.
beats.narration_text: Here's the author's hand-written effect. It's a canvas item shader, because the gauges are 2D drawing inside a sub-viewport. Three uniforms: night amount, driven from code; a warm amber colour; and a brightness floor. Line 14 is the whole effect. It mixes the original colour toward that colour times amber times brightness. Multiplying keeps the gauge detail, and mix lets it fade.

beats.role_note: Result of B04: controlled-value captures against the hand predictions.
beats.narration_text: Big idea one: a shader is a small program the GPU runs for every pixel. Line 14 runs once per dashboard pixel, so its output can be predicted. The brief predicted two pixels by hand, the dark background and the dial hub, at three settings. The engine captures match all eighteen numbers exactly. At two point zero, set from code, the hub goes almost black: hint range draws a slider, but it doesn't clamp.

beats.role_note: Prediction method typeset with TypesetMath (MATH-TYPESETTING.md).
beats.narration_text: Here's the hand calculation. Factor the mix, and each channel is the original value times one minus the amount, plus the amount times amber times brightness. For the hub's red channel at one half, that's 135 times zero point seven seven five: one hundred and four point six two five, which rounds to 105. The capture reads 105.

beats.role_note: Code beat: the dimming driver; complete input -> state -> output trace in notes.
beats.narration_text: The driver is GDScript written by Claude Code, and it only reads the van's headlights flag. It never sets it. Each frame, it moves night amount toward its target by delta over the fade time, so the speed doesn't depend on frame rate. A retrigger simply reverses from wherever the value is. Once it arrives, lines 25 and 26 stop sending updates.

beats.role_note: Code beat: where the two fog materials attach.
beats.narration_text: The textured shader goes on two new overlays, built beside the existing glass, never in place of it. The windshield gets the light fog material. The driver's window gets the heavy fog material, and because that overlay is a child of the window pane, it inherits every move the pane makes.

props.title: Two Overlays, One Shader
props.source: Godot editor reconstruction · game/features/vehicles/freight_van/van_presentation.gd:226–233 · written by Claude Code · code shown verbatim

	var pane := Build.instance(_cabin, Vector3(0, 2.17, -1.34), windshield, _glass)
	pane.rotation.x = 0.32
	fog_overlays.append(_fog_overlay(pane, windshield.size, Vector3(0, 0, 0.012), 0.0,
		LIGHT_FOG))
	fog_overlays.append(_fog_overlay(_windows[0], Vector2(1.48, 0.9), Vector3(0.012, 0, 0),
		PI / 2, HEAVY_FOG))

beats.role_note: Code beat: the fog shader's interface (types, hints, defaults, groups).
beats.narration_text: The fog shader is spatial, because the glass is in 3D. Its render mode blends it over the scene, skips depth writes, and draws both faces. Seven uniforms sit in three Inspector groups, each with a type, a range and a default. Big idea four: group uniforms, hint range and source colour aren't plain G L S L. They're Godot's shading language talking to the editor.

beats.role_note: Result of B11: the interface sweep.
beats.narration_text: The sweep runs every control at its minimum, default and maximum on the windshield, then measures what changed. Fog amount is the big one: at its maximum, eight percent of the frame changes and the pane clouds over. Clear centre at zero lets fog creep in from the corner. The other five barely move a pixel, because at the light default the fog band sits behind the frame. To judge them, the next sweep needs a heavier base fog.

beats.role_note: Code beat: the three samplers and the data read.
beats.narration_text: Three textures, three jobs. Fog colour has source colour, so Godot decodes it as colour. Fog normal has hint normal: these are directions, not colours. Fog data has no hint at all, and line 35 reads only its red channel, as a thickness from zero to one. Big idea three: a texture is information, not just a picture.

beats.narration_text: Here are the three files. A seeded script written by Claude Code generated them, so they're original and reproducible. Their import settings are written down explicitly: lossless, mipmaps on, normal-map mode set by hand. That's why opening the editor later didn't change them. And a curl check against a known Poly Haven pair confirms the normal map's green channel points up, the convention Godot expects.

beats.role_note: Code beat: the material resource.
beats.narration_text: A material holds settings, not the program. Light fog points at the same shader and the same three textures, then sets its own values. Heavy fog differs in exactly four of them. Big idea two: the shader declares fog amount once, on line 7, and each material gives it its own value: a quarter here, three quarters on the side window.

beats.narration_text: Side by side: light fog on the windshield, heavy fog on the driver's window. Change one value in the light fog material, and only the windshield clouds over, because materials don't share values. Now turn that fog up so it shows, and change one line of the shader: both windows turn red, because they share the program. Two edits, and the difference between a material and a shader is on screen.

beats.role_note: Code beat: the hint-experiment shader.
beats.narration_text: The hint experiment isolates a single word. A tiny image holds three grey bands: 64, 128 and 192. The author's shader reads it through two samplers, one with source colour and one without, and a show data switch picks which one an unshaded quad displays. Same file, same pixels, one hint different.

props.title: One Hint, Isolated
props.source: Godot editor reconstruction · game/shaders/hint_experiment.gdshader:1–16 · hand-written by the author · code shown verbatim

notes.label: Input image
notes.value: greys_3x1.png: 64 · 128 · 192 (tools/make_hint_png.gd)

notes.label: Unshaded
notes.value: render_mode unshaded: no lighting changes the value

beats.role_note: Result of B17: hint experiment predicted vs measured, two renderers.
beats.narration_text: The prediction: read as colour, each band is decoded to linear light and encoded back on the way out, so it stays 64, 128 and 192. Read as data, the raw value is only encoded: 137, 188 and 225. A Forward Plus comparison matched that exactly. But in Compatibility, the game's renderer, both quads showed the file's values. Same shader, different renderer, different numbers.

props.title: Same Shader, Two Renderers
props.label: Held frames · engine captures at 3840 × 2160, scripted · markers show the sampled data-quad values

beats.role_note: sRGB encode typeset (MATH-TYPESETTING.md); algebra checked in FACTCHECK.md.
beats.narration_text: Here's the encode the prediction used. Above a tiny threshold, the stored value is one point zero five five times the linear value to the power one over two point four, minus zero point zero five five. Feed in 64 over 255, about zero point two five one, and you get about zero point five three eight: 137.

props.title: The Encode Behind 137
props.note: Read as data, the stored value is encoded once on output.
props.conditions: For x ≤ 0.0031308 the encode is 12.92 x instead. 128 → 188 and 192 → 225 follow the same way.

beats.role_note: Code beat: two annotated generated lines beside the author's equivalents.
beats.narration_text: To learn the language, the author converted a standard material into a shader and annotated what Godot generated. Lines 6 and 7: an albedo colour and an albedo texture, both marked source colour. The author's equivalents are fog tint, on line 9, and fog colour, on line 26. They make the same promise: these values are colours, so decode them.

beats.role_note: Result of B20: the same textures through Godot's generated shader and the author's shader.
beats.narration_text: Here are the same texture files through both shaders. Godot's generated shader paints the colour texture onto an opaque, lit surface, and the normal map raises tiny bumps. The author's shader turns them into fog: the data texture makes it patchy, and alpha lets the stripes behind it show through. The generated code teaches the vocabulary; the hand-written shader decides what the textures mean.

beats.role_note: Code beat: a test excerpt.
beats.narration_text: Tests get their own look. This is Claude Code's driver test asking Godot for the shader's uniform list. If the shader fails to parse, that list comes back empty, so one check catches a broken shader. Other checks press the real L key through Godot's input system and sample night amount on every frame.
